example: Example: A regulation requiring every AI company to publish the energy consumed to train each major model, and mandating that data centres running AI must source 100% renewable electricity within three years — creating transparency and legal obligations for a sector that currently reports neither.

def: Requiring that data centres powering AI systems source 100% of their electricity from renewable energy through direct power purchase agreements, on-site generation, or verified green tariff contracts.
example: Example: A law requiring tech companies to prove their data centres run on renewable electricity — through contracts with wind and solar farms, on-site generation, or time-matched renewable certificates — rather than offsetting fossil fuel use with distant carbon credits.

def: Regulating AI model training and deployment to meet improving energy efficiency standards — measured in computations per watt — driving innovation in energy-efficient AI architecture and hardware.
example: Example: A standard requiring AI models above a certain size to demonstrate they use no more than a set amount of energy per billion parameters — pushing hardware makers and AI labs to prioritise efficiency alongside capability in their development roadmaps.

def: Requiring independent audits of AI systems used in sustainability reporting and ESG disclosures, with traceability requirements that enable verification of AI-generated claims about environmental performance.
example: Example: A financial regulation requiring that any ESG report produced with AI assistance must be independently audited to verify the AI's sources, methods, and outputs — making it illegal to publish AI-generated sustainability claims without a human expert signing off on their accuracy.

def: Developing standardised third-party verification requirements for ESG data and reports, with penalties for unverifiable or misleading claims regardless of whether they were AI-generated.
example: Example: A mandatory standard requiring all ESG metrics to be verified by an accredited third party using standardised methodologies — so investors can trust that a company's reported carbon emissions are real figures, not AI-generated estimates tuned to look good.

def: Passing legislation requiring transparency in AI-generated content, with mandatory labelling of AI-produced media and liability for organisations deploying AI to deceive in regulated domains.
example: Example: A law requiring that any image, video, or report generated by AI and used in financial or environmental disclosures must be clearly labelled as AI-generated — and making companies liable if AI-produced content is used to mislead investors or regulators.

def: Requiring comprehensive environmental and ecological impact assessments for AI systems deployed in extractive industries, logistics, agriculture, and urban planning before deployment.
example: Example: Before an AI system that optimises mining operations can be deployed, its developer must complete a formal assessment of its likely impact on ecosystem disturbance, water use, and carbon emissions — reviewed by an independent environmental body.

def: Imposing moratoriums on new fossil fuel and mineral extraction projects that rely on AI to access previously uneconomical reserves, pending assessment of climate and ecological impact.
example: Example: A ban on new deep-sea mining projects that use AI-powered underwater robots to access mineral deposits — until global environmental impact assessments are completed and international standards are agreed, none can proceed.

def: Establishing policy frameworks requiring AI systems used in land use, transport, and agriculture to incorporate biodiversity and ecological constraints into their decision-making rather than optimising purely for economic output.
example: Example: A requirement that AI systems used in agricultural planning must incorporate habitat maps and species data as mandatory inputs — so an AI recommending field expansions must account for the protected wildflower meadow in its calculations, not just crop yield.

def: Requiring periodic audits of AI systems deployed in nature-affecting sectors to assess their ecological footprint, unintended wildlife impacts, and compliance with nature-positive standards.
example: Example: Every two years, any AI system managing forestry, fisheries, or agriculture operations must submit to an independent audit that checks whether its real-world decisions are producing the ecological outcomes claimed when it was deployed.

def: Developing and mandating design standards for AI systems that incorporate ecological data as core inputs alongside economic variables — ensuring algorithms can't optimise for profit while systematically ignoring nature.
example: Example: A design standard requiring logistics AI systems to include road kill data, noise impact on wildlife corridors, and habitat fragmentation scores in their route optimisation calculations — not just speed and fuel cost.

def: Developing standardised frameworks for assessing the environmental impact of AI systems across their full lifecycle — training energy, deployment infrastructure, induced activity effects, and ecological consequences of decisions made.
example: Example: A standardised scorecard that every AI company must complete for major models, covering: energy used in training, projected energy used in deployment, the sectors it will affect, and the anticipated environmental consequences of the decisions it will automate.

def: Creating international open-source systems for verifying AI-generated climate models, with transparent audit trails, shared validation datasets, and independent scientific review of model outputs.
example: Example: A global open-source platform where climate models from any country can be submitted for independent validation — scientists worldwide can inspect the code, check the training data, and verify the outputs, making manipulation immediately visible.

def: Negotiating a binding international treaty that prohibits adversarial attacks on scientific AI systems, establishes norms for AI security in climate research, and creates verification mechanisms.
example: Example: An international treaty — similar to the Chemical Weapons Convention — that makes it illegal for any nation or organisation to attempt to corrupt or manipulate AI systems used in global climate monitoring and modelling.

def: Deploying cryptographic and federated learning protocols that ensure the integrity of shared climate AI models — detecting data poisoning and ensuring no single actor can manipulate shared global climate model outputs.
example: Example: A cryptographic system where every update to a shared global climate model is signed by multiple independent research institutions — if any one party tries to insert manipulated data, the signatures won't match and the tampering is automatically flagged.

def: Creating a global commons of open-source AI climate tools — flood prediction, crop advisory, extreme weather modelling — freely accessible to all nations regardless of technical or financial capacity.
example: Example: A UN-funded platform offering free AI-powered flood prediction tools, drought early warning systems, and crop advisory services to any country — a small Pacific island nation gets access to the same AI forecasting technology as a wealthy European government.

def: Requiring wealthy nations and technology companies to transfer clean and climate adaptation technologies — including AI systems — to developing nations on preferential or free terms.
example: Example: A trade agreement requiring signatories to share patents and technical knowledge for clean energy and climate adaptation technologies with the 50 least developed countries at no cost — ensuring technology doesn't stay locked up in wealthy countries while climate-vulnerable nations lack tools to adapt.

def: Funding programmes that build AI capacity in Global South nations — training data scientists, developing locally appropriate AI tools, and creating infrastructure for climate AI deployment.
example: Example: An international fund that trains 1,000 AI specialists in climate-vulnerable countries, funds the development of AI tools specific to local farming conditions and language contexts, and connects graduates to global climate AI research networks.

def: Activating emergency international cooperation frameworks to coordinate global response to simultaneous climate crises — pooling resources, expertise, and political will across nations for collective action.
example: Example: When simultaneous droughts and floods devastate food production across three continents simultaneously, an emergency UN framework coordinates the rapid redistribution of global food reserves, medical teams, and financial aid — treating it as a shared emergency rather than separate national problems.

def: Pursuing fundamental transformation of economic, energy, and food systems — not incremental improvement but redesign of the underlying structures that generate environmental crisis in the first place.
example: Example: Not just building more electric cars, but redesigning cities so people don't need cars; not just making farming slightly less destructive, but building food systems that regenerate ecosystems — transforming the system rather than adjusting its parameters.

def: Reforming international governance institutions — UN, WTO, IMF, World Bank — to centre climate action, equity, and planetary boundaries in all decision-making rather than treating them as secondary to economic growth.
example: Example: Reforming the World Bank's mandate to prohibit financing of any fossil fuel infrastructure globally, and requiring all IMF loans to include climate resilience conditions — so the most powerful financial institutions in the world work for climate stability rather than against it.

def: Adopting a planetary stewardship framework across governance at all scales — where human economic activity is designed to operate within Earth's ecological limits rather than continuously extracting beyond them.
example: Example: A national constitution amended to enshrine the rights of nature alongside the rights of citizens — so economic development plans must legally demonstrate they stay within ecological boundaries before they can be approved.

def: Coordinating the complete transformation of human civilisation's relationship with the planet — energy, food, economy, governance, and culture — toward sustainable coexistence within planetary boundaries.
example: Example: The entire reorientation of a society's economy — from measuring success by GDP growth to measuring it by wellbeing and ecological health, from fossil fuels to clean energy, from extraction to regeneration — happening across all sectors simultaneously over a generation.

def: Emergency-level binding international climate agreements that go beyond standard treaty frameworks — committing all major emitters to immediate and radical emission cuts under conditions of planetary emergency.
example: Example: An emergency climate summit triggered by evidence of AMOC weakening, at which the world's twenty largest emitting nations commit to halving emissions within five years with binding enforcement mechanisms — treating climate as the existential emergency it is.
